text:
At 2:40 a.m., the scent of rising yeast always fought the smell of floor wax. Arthur wiped his flour-dusted hands on his apron and approached the wire cooling racks. There, resting between two wicker proofing baskets, sat a battered paperback copy of *The Count of Monte Cristo*. 

It was the fourth Thursday in a row. The first time, Arthur thought a customer had simply forgotten it. But every week, the exact same library book reappeared on the rack, always with its spine aligned perfectly with the edge of the metal shelf. 

Arthur picked it up. Tonight, a yellow sticky note clung to the cover. Written in elegant, shaky cursive, it read: *The baker in chapter five reminds me of you. Thank you for keeping the lights on.*

Arthur stared at the note, his thumb smoothing the creased paper. The bakery was silent save for the low hum of the refrigeration units. He didn't know who the late-night reader was, but he knew the book was due back at the municipal library down the street.

Arthur walked to the prep table, took a still-warm cinnamon roll, wrapped it carefully in parchment paper, and tucked it into his coat pocket to drop off at the library book return on his walk home.

The sourdough was on its second rise when I found it. Again. 

It’s always a Thursday, always right on the flour bin, and always a copy of *The Count of Monte Cristo* with the Richmond Public Library stamp. I don't know how they get past the squeaky screen door without me hearing, but frankly, around 3:00 AM, my brain is mostly yeast and caffeine anyway. 

Tonight, though, a scrap of yellow legal paper was poking out of the top like a bookmark. 

I wiped my hands on my apron, leaving a ghostly white smudge on the dark cloth, and pulled it out. *Page 142,* the note said in frantic, spiky handwriting. *Please. I think they’re watching the drop box now.* 

A cold draft swept through the kitchen, smelling of wet asphalt and oncoming rain. I looked toward the darkened front windows, but all I saw was my own tired reflection staring back. 

I didn't open the book. Instead, I carefully tucked the note back between the pages, slid the novel into a brown pastry bag, and folded the top down twice to seal it.

Flour dust settled like frost over the stainless-steel prep table. At 3:15 a.m., Arthur found the book. It sat beside the sourdough starter, exactly where he had found a different library volume every Thursday for a month. 

Tonight’s book was a battered copy of *The Birds of eastern North America*. Arthur picked it up, leaving a white thumbprint on the fabric spine. The library stamp on the pocket inside showed it was three weeks overdue. 

He flipped the pages. A slip of blue lined paper fluttered out onto the floury table. 

*The yeast in my kitchen won’t rise,* the pencil handwriting read. *I am trying your method. Page 112.*

Arthur turned to page 112. The margins were clean, but someone had pressed a single, dried hop blossom flat against the illustration of a cedar waxwing. 

Arthur smelled the paper. It carried the faint, bitter scent of wild fermentation, not the sterile scent of the library. He tucked the note into his apron pocket. He walked to the back of the kitchen, scooped a cup of active, bubbling rye starter into a clean glass jar, and pressed a square of cheesecloth over the lid with a rubber band.

At 2:40 a.m., the sour tang of fermenting rye always overtook the floor bleach. Arthur wiped his palms on his jeans and reached behind the wicker bannetons. Resting on the bottom wire rack was the library’s taped-up copy of *The Count of Monte Cristo*. 

The fourth Thursday. Like the others, its spine ran flush with the steel edge. 

He pulled it free. Stuck to the cover was a square of blue prescription notepad. Written in ballpoint ink that had pressed through the paper: *The baker in chapter five reminds me of you. Thank you for keeping the lights on.*

Arthur’s thumb traced the deep indentation of the pen strokes. The only sound was the shudder of the compressor. From the back of the book, a slip of paper drifted down—a yellowing due-date card stamped in faded red ink, three days overdue. 

Arthur walked to the prep table, wrapped a warm, glaze-mapped cinnamon roll in parchment paper, and slipped it into his coat pocket alongside the book.
